title: RAG Overview
content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, often abbreviated as RAG, is an approach that combines a language model with an external retrieval mechanism. Instead of relying only on the information stored in model parameters during training, a RAG system retrieves relevant documents at inference time and uses them as context for answer generation. This can improve factual grounding, reduce hallucinations, and make responses more transparent because the model can be linked to specific retrieved sources.

title: RAG Workflow
content: A typical RAG workflow consists of several steps. First, a user submits a query. Second, the system converts that query into an embedding representation. Third, the embedding is compared against embeddings stored in a vector database in order to retrieve semantically relevant documents. Finally, the retrieved documents are injected into a prompt and passed to the language model, which generates the answer. This workflow allows the model to combine generation with external knowledge access.

title: Purpose of RAG
content: The main purpose of Retrieval-Augmented Generation is to reduce hallucinations and improve reliability. A standard language model may generate answers that sound plausible but are not grounded in verifiable sources. RAG addresses this by providing the model with relevant external information before generation. This makes it more likely that the answer is based on retrieved evidence instead of unsupported associations learned during training.

title: RAG and Factual Accuracy
content: One of the main advantages of RAG is improved factual accuracy. By retrieving relevant passages from an external collection, the model can answer with information that is more specific and more current than its internal parametric memory alone. This is especially useful in domains where precision matters or where the model needs access to information that was not explicitly memorized during training.

title: RAG Limitations
content: Although RAG can improve answer quality, it also has limitations. If retrieval returns irrelevant or misleading documents, the final answer may still be poor. In addition, retrieval adds computational cost and system complexity. A RAG system may also retrieve too much context, which can introduce noise into the prompt. Therefore, the quality of retrieval is a critical factor in overall system performance.

title: Grounded Responses
content: A grounded response is an answer that is supported by retrieved or otherwise verifiable evidence. In RAG systems, grounding usually means that the generated answer is based on external documents that were selected because they are relevant to the query. Grounding is important because it makes the reasoning path more transparent and can help reduce unsupported claims.

title: Retrieval Step
content: The retrieval step in a RAG system is responsible for selecting documents that are semantically relevant to the user query. This is typically done by comparing vector embeddings of the query and the stored documents. The top-k most similar documents are then returned. If retrieval is weak, the language model may receive poor context and generate weak answers even if the generator itself is capable.

title: Generation Step
content: After relevant documents are retrieved, the generation step uses them as additional context for the language model. The model does not simply copy the documents. Instead, it uses them to generate a fluent answer that incorporates the retrieved information. The quality of the final answer depends on both the relevance of the retrieved material and the model's ability to integrate that material coherently.

title: Top-K Retrieval
content: Top-k retrieval refers to the practice of returning the k most relevant documents for a query. A small k may reduce noise but risks missing useful context. A large k may increase recall but can introduce irrelevant information. Choosing a suitable top-k value is therefore an important design decision in RAG systems and can directly affect answer quality.

title: Prompt Construction with Retrieved Context
content: In RAG systems, retrieved documents are often inserted into a prompt before the user question. The structure of this prompt matters. A well-designed prompt can encourage the language model to use the provided evidence, stay close to the retrieved context, and avoid inventing unsupported details. Poor prompt construction may reduce the benefits of retrieval even if the correct documents were found.

title: LLM Context Window Limitation
content: A large language model has a limited context window, meaning it can only process a certain amount of text at once. Information outside that window cannot be directly considered during generation. This limitation motivates external retrieval, because relevant information can be selected and inserted into the context instead of expecting the model to store everything internally.

title: Static Model Knowledge
content: A standard language model relies on knowledge acquired during training. This knowledge is static in the sense that the model cannot directly access new or external data unless a retrieval or tool mechanism is added. As a result, the model may produce outdated or incomplete answers when asked about information that is not well represented in its training data.

title: LLM Hallucinations
content: Hallucinations occur when a language model generates information that sounds convincing but is false, unsupported, or not grounded in real evidence. Hallucinations are one of the major reliability problems in generative AI. Techniques such as retrieval, tool use, and structured prompting are often introduced to reduce the frequency of hallucinated answers.

title: External Knowledge Access
content: External knowledge access allows a language model to go beyond its internal training data. This can include retrieving documents from a vector database, calling APIs, querying structured databases, or accessing tools through a protocol. External access is important when the task requires up-to-date, domain-specific, or verifiable information.

title: Why Retrieval Helps
content: Retrieval helps because it gives the language model access to focused context that is relevant to the current question. Instead of expecting the model to infer everything from internal weights, the system can provide concrete passages that narrow the search space during generation. This often improves specificity, grounding, and consistency.

title: MCP Definition
content: The Model Context Protocol, often abbreviated as MCP, is a protocol-oriented concept for structured interaction between language models and external resources. Instead of treating tool use as an informal add-on, MCP-style approaches aim to standardize how models request tools, receive results, and incorporate those results into a response. This supports more modular and extensible system design.

title: MCP and Tool Integration
content: An MCP-oriented system can connect a language model to external tools such as retrieval systems, databases, search mechanisms, or APIs. The key idea is that the model does not only generate text, but can also interact with a structured tool layer. This makes it possible to extend the model with new capabilities while keeping the interaction pattern organized and reusable.

title: Structured Tool Calls
content: Structured tool calls are an important idea in MCP-like architectures. Instead of letting the model freely produce unstructured commands, the system defines a clear interface for tools. This makes the interaction more reliable because inputs and outputs are standardized. It also simplifies debugging and evaluation, since tool usage can be tracked explicitly.

title: Selective Retrieval
content: Selective retrieval means that a system does not retrieve external documents for every question. Instead, it first decides whether retrieval is necessary. This can reduce latency, lower system cost, and avoid injecting irrelevant context into prompts. Selective retrieval is useful because not every question benefits from external evidence. Simple arithmetic or basic general knowledge may not require retrieval at all.

title: Always-On Retrieval versus Selective Retrieval
content: A traditional RAG pipeline often performs retrieval for every user query. This can improve grounding but may also lead to unnecessary retrieval for simple questions. In contrast, a selective retrieval system first decides whether external context is needed. This creates an interesting trade-off: always-on retrieval may be more consistently grounded, while selective retrieval may be more efficient and less noisy.

title: Modularity in LLM Systems
content: Modularity refers to the degree to which system components can be separated, replaced, and extended independently. In a modular LLM system, the language model, retriever, storage layer, and orchestration logic can be treated as separate components. This is beneficial for research prototypes because it supports experimentation and makes the system architecture easier to analyze.

title: Extensibility
content: Extensibility describes how easily a system can be extended with new components or capabilities. In the context of a RAG and MCP-inspired prototype, extensibility might involve adding new tools, changing the vector database, replacing the embedding model, or integrating a different generator. A well-structured prototype should make such changes relatively straightforward.

title: Reproducibility
content: Reproducibility is important in research-oriented system design. A reproducible prototype should be runnable by another person with the same code, dependencies, documents, and configuration. Logging retrieved documents, decisions, and timings helps make experiments more transparent. Reproducibility is especially important when comparing baseline, RAG, and MCP-style approaches.

title: Reliability Evaluation
content: Reliability in this prototype context refers to whether the system produces answers that are correct, grounded, and consistent. Evaluation can compare a baseline model without retrieval, a RAG system with automatic retrieval, and an MCP-like system with selective retrieval. Relevant criteria may include correctness, groundedness, retrieval usage, and the quality of the retrieved documents.

title: Baseline versus RAG
content: A baseline language model answers only from its internal knowledge and prompt context. A RAG system, in contrast, retrieves additional documents before generation. Comparing the two can show whether retrieval improves answer quality, reduces hallucinations, or changes response behavior. Such a comparison is useful in research prototypes that investigate reliability.

title: Baseline versus MCP-Like Retrieval
content: A comparison between a baseline language model and an MCP-like retrieval pipeline can highlight the value of structured external access. The baseline may answer quickly but without grounding in local documents. An MCP-inspired system can decide when retrieval is worth using, which may improve efficiency while still enabling grounded answers for domain-specific questions.

title: Vector Database
content: A vector database stores embeddings of documents so that semantically similar items can be retrieved efficiently. In a simple prototype, each document is embedded once and stored together with an identifier and metadata. At query time, the user question is embedded and compared to the stored document vectors. The database then returns the most similar entries.

title: Embeddings
content: Embeddings are numerical vector representations of text. They map semantically similar content to nearby points in vector space. In retrieval systems, embeddings are used to compare queries and documents even when they do not share the exact same wording. This is one reason why embedding-based retrieval can work better than strict keyword matching for natural language queries.

title: Domain-Specific Knowledge
content: One of the strongest use cases for retrieval is domain-specific knowledge. A general-purpose language model may know broad concepts, but it may not reliably reproduce the exact definitions, terminology, or constraints that matter in a particular project. A local document collection can provide domain-specific context that aligns the response with the intended knowledge base.

title: Noise in Retrieved Context
content: Not every retrieved document is helpful. If the retriever returns partially relevant or irrelevant passages, the language model may become distracted or combine correct and incorrect details. This problem is often described as retrieval noise. Selective retrieval and better ranking strategies can help reduce such noise.

title: Neural Networks Overview
content: Neural networks are computational models inspired by biological nervous systems. They consist of layers of interconnected units that transform input data into output representations. Neural networks are widely used in tasks such as image classification, speech recognition, and natural language processing. Although they are relevant to AI in general, they are not the same as retrieval-augmented generation.

title: Computer Vision Basics
content: Computer vision focuses on enabling machines to interpret visual data such as images and video. Typical applications include object detection, segmentation, pose estimation, and facial recognition. While computer vision also uses machine learning and neural networks, it is largely unrelated to the core mechanics of RAG and MCP-oriented text retrieval prototypes.

title: Autonomous Vehicles
content: Autonomous vehicles use sensors, mapping, control systems, and machine learning to navigate without constant human control. Their development involves computer vision, sensor fusion, planning, and safety engineering. This topic is useful as a distractor document in a retrieval experiment because it is clearly within AI but does not directly answer questions about RAG or MCP.

title: Medical Imaging
content: Medical imaging includes modalities such as MRI, CT, ultrasound, and X-ray. Machine learning can support classification, segmentation, and anomaly detection in medical images. Although this is an important AI application area, it is not directly relevant to a local document collection focused on retrieval-augmented generation and tool-oriented LLM prototypes.

title: Image Classification
content: Image classification is the task of assigning a label to an image, such as identifying whether it contains a dog, a car, or a medical abnormality. Convolutional neural networks are often used for this problem. This document is intentionally included as a distractor because it belongs to machine learning but does not explain RAG or MCP.

title: Prototype Goal
content: The goal of the prototype is to compare three answer generation modes: a baseline language model without retrieval, a RAG pipeline with automatic retrieval, and an MCP-inspired pipeline with selective retrieval. The prototype focuses on reliability, modularity, extensibility, and reproducibility rather than on large-scale production deployment.

title: Prototype Architecture
content: The prototype architecture consists of a local language model, an embedding model, a vector database, a retrieval function, and an orchestration layer. In the baseline configuration, the language model answers directly. In the RAG configuration, retrieval is always performed. In the MCP-inspired configuration, the system decides whether retrieval is needed before generating an answer.

title: Research Question Context
content: A central research motivation behind the prototype is whether structured external retrieval can improve the reliability of LLM-based answers while maintaining modularity and extensibility. The comparison between baseline, RAG, and MCP-like retrieval is designed to explore whether selective access to local knowledge sources produces better controlled responses.
